`
Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Monday, 26 February 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 010)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting_
Mr Dan Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Lachlan Gyles SC with Ms Joanna Davidson for NSW Health

MR MUSTON: Good morning, Commissioner. We are moving now
to the innovation phase of this hearing block. There will
obviously be some overlap between what we're discussing
this morning and some of the procurement issues that were
raised last week, but that's where we're at.
I do think we have a formal tender of some
confidential documents and an order that needs to be made
in respect of confidentiality but I won't deal with that
immediately.
THE COMMISSIONER: Okay.
MR MUSTON: Ms Waterhouse is going to deal with this
witness.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
DR WATERHOUSE: Commissioner, the witness is already in
the witness box. It is Adjunct Professor Jéan-Fredéric
Levesque. I will spell his name in full for the court
reporter, J-É-A-N-hyphen-F-R-É-D-E-R-I-C L-E-V-E-S-Q-U-E.
<JÉAN-FREDÉRIC LEVESQUE, affirmed: [10.01am]
<EXAMINATION BY DR WATERHOUSE:
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. Dr Levesque, can you please state
your full name and also your occupation?
A. My name is Jéan-Fredéric Levesque, I'm deputy
secretary for clinical innovation and research in
NSW Health and I'm the chief executive of the Agency for
Clinical Innovation, also within NSW Health.
Q. How long have you been in this role?
A. I've been in the role of deputy secretary for
12 months and I've been the chief executive of the Agency
for Clinical Innovation for a little bit less than six
years.
Q. And what roles have you held before that?
A. Within NSW Health I've also been chief executive of
the Bureau of Health Information and previously I had
various professional roles in Canada, before migrating to
Australia.
Q. And can you outline for us your qualifications?

A. I'm a medical doctor by training. I've got
a specialisation in preventive medicine and public health
and I'm a fellow of the Royal College of Physicians and
Surgeons of Canada and I also have a PhD in public health
from University of Montreal.
Q. Thank you. You have prepared a statement to assist
the Commission, and I believe that statement is dated
30 January 2024. You have a copy of the statement with
you?
A. Yes, I do.
DR WATERHOUSE: We might just bring that up on the screen,
if we could, it is exhibit B.003 [MOH.0001.0435.0001].
Q. Have you had a chance to review the statement before
giving evidence today?
A. Yes.
Q. And is the content true and correct to the best of
your knowledge and belief?
A. Yes, it is.
Q. We might scroll down to paragraph 4. In that
paragraph you refer to the creation of the clinical
innovation and research division approximately one year
ago, February 2023. What was the rationale for developing
this or establishing this division and what do you see as
the advantages?
A. There were various goals in establishing the division,
bringing together the Office for Health and Medical
Research and the Agency for Clinical Innovation and the
first one was really to lift research and innovation as
a key priority for NSW Health, really send the signal that
it is an important component of the system and something
that we need to continue to progress.
There was also a desire to better coordinate the work
across the entire continuum from research, discoveries and
implementation in the real healthcare system. So the
objectives were really to ensure that we would have more
visibility from a research perspective and also really
align our work for stronger impact on the system.
Q. Can you see any disadvantages to creating it as
a division in the ministry?
A. I don't see any disadvantages. I think that it's

really creating an opportunity for better aligning our
investments in research with the efforts that we're making
to translate them into clinical practice.
The only thing that we need to manage as part of this
arrangement is the fact that the Agency for Clinical
Innovation is a pillar of NSW Health and therefore, you
know, we've had to establish different ways to manage
a pillar and branches of the ministry, working together,
but again, it's a great opportunity to actually be able to
make a pillar work so closely with branches of the
ministry, it was just a matter of establishing the right
governance processes.
Q. One of the terms of reference --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Sorry, so the division of clinical
innovation and research is part of the Ministry of Health?
A. It is.
Q. So the ACI and the Office for Health and Medical
Research, it says, "were integrated to form a new
division". I don't quite - the ACI still stands alone as
a pillar - yes?
A. Yes, it does.
Q. And there's the Office for Health and Medical
Research - that stands alone as an office?
A. It's one of the branches, yes.
Q. And what is the form of integration to form this
division of clinical innovation and research?
A. Well, the first thing, Commissioner, is that both of
those units are led by the same person, myself.
Q. That's you?
A. So I'm deputy secretary, you know, supervising all of
the research and innovation work across the system for
NSW Health and I'm the chief executive of the Agency for
Clinical Innovation. So in this way, there was a first
level of integration. And then from a functional
perspective, the management structures within ACI as well
as OHMR and the small structures that enable me to lead the
division in a more coordinated way all meet together in
planning our activities. There is --
Q. There might be a really good reason for this, and this

is your chance to tell us why, it just sounds like it
should be the one organisation. The division of clinical
innovation sounds a lot like the Agency for Clinical
Innovation. Obviously I'm missing something as to why it's
been done this way as distinct from just all of these three
entities being the one organisation.
A. The Agency for Clinical Innovation as a pillar
organisation, like other pillars, has a role to provide
advice to the ministry, provide advice to the system in an
impartial way, as pillar organisation, and that arm's
length role was seen as an advantage in keeping the agency
as a separate entity from a legal perspective, but really
aligning it through its leadership with the work of OHMR,
the work of the critical intelligence unit, within
a division so that we better coordinate the work.
So we were trying to preserve the advantages and the
levers that are part of a pillar organisation but by
bringing it under a more integrated leadership so that it
would really span the entire continuum from grant delivery
to working with clinicians through that independent entity
for real system change. But really, from a functional
perspective, we now have meetings that enable us to
coordinate the work across the two organisations.
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. The Commissioner asked if the OHMR,
or Office for Health and Medical Research, was
a stand-alone body and I think you responded that it was
a branch. Is it, in fact, a branch of the ministry?
A. It's a branch of the division for clinical innovation
and research, so, yes, it is a branch of the Ministry of
Health, from a legal perspective.
Q. So the only part that sort of stands alone,
effectively, is the ACI?
A. That is correct.
Q. Thank you. Part of the terms of reference for this
Inquiry is to inquire into the balance between central
oversight and locally devolved decision-making. Could
bringing the ACI and the OHMR together in this way, into
the division in the ministry, be seen as an increase in
centralisation?
A. I think to answer that question, I need to reflect on
what kind of organisation the ACI is. I think it is
important, because you'll see that the ACI is an
organisation that is already heavily decentralised through

its clinical networks.
So the agency has, you know, employees that we
directly employ, they include network managers, they
include people that have expertise in epidemiology just or
organisational studies, data analysis, but the agency, one
of its core roles is to lead 42 clinical networks that are
made of clinicians working in local districts, working in
our different hospitals across the system.
And the number of core fluctuates, but there are
thousands of clinicians involved in various groups led by
those clinical networks, and that really is a way for us to
reach very deeply into the system, making sure that we hear
from real clinicians, you know, currently working in the
system about issues that may need to be addressed, or about
opportunities in terms of new ways to deliver care, and
then bringing it within an organisation that then can
mobilise resources to redesign models or to support
implementation at the state level.
So the ACI is already a very, you know, decentralised
structure with that reaching out of clinicians through our
work.
One of the goals of establishing the division was
actually to make sure that we would keep that clinical
voice and bring it to the ministry executive so that the
ACI being part of or led in an integrated way as part of
that division for clinical innovation and research, then we
could create that, you know, streamlined channel so that
the voice of clinicians could be conveyed to the ministry
executive in an even more effective way going forward
So I think the reality is that it's not a top-down
approach; it's not just a bottom-up approach either. It's
about balancing those two together so that we have really
activities in the system but in a way that it can then get
into policies and in more integrated and statewide
approaches. That's one of the advantages of having
established a division as it stands, because we can keep
that really essential role of mobilising thousands of
clinicians for the purpose of innovation, and then
integrated to inform policy that is led at the central
level as well.
Q. Would it be fair to say that the decentralisation that

you're referring to there relates to consultation rather
than the actual decision-making being on the ground, and
that the decision-making is done more centrally by ACI?
A. There has not been any changes following the creation
of the division with regards to how ACI makes its
decisions. We have clinical networks executive committees
and these are made of doctor, nurses, allied health
professionals and consumers. They identify the work that
they need to do and then have it endorsed by the ACI
executive committee. And we also have a clinical executive
advisory group that informs the decisions of ACI, and we're
talking about clinicians from intensive care, surgery,
primary care, many different areas.
The ACI still has, as it had in the past,
a performance agreement with the Ministry of Health,
identifying what are the key priorities, what is the work
that is emerging from the different networks that we need
to bring to scale, and that has not changed following the
establishment of the division. So we've really tried
again, as part of that transformation, to keep the strong
advantages of the current structure, making sure that the
voice of clinicians is well coordinated, well supported by
the ACI, but by having a deputy secretary that leads that
agency, you know, interacts with the clinical networks on
a regular basis through our own ACI mechanic, then I can
bring that clinical voice to the ministry executive, and
that was one of the objectives as part of that reform of
our structures.
Q. I'm going to come back to the ACI in more detail a
little bit later. I would like to ask you some questions
now about the Office for Health and Medical Research. So
if we could just scroll down to paragraph 14, please.
Before we go to that, can you just describe for us the
purpose and functions of the Office for Health and Medical
Research?
A. Yes. So the Office for Health and Medical Research
has got, as overarching role, to catalyse research into
NSW Health through different ways. Its role is really to
be a central agency that helps local districts, hospitals,
to use and produce research for the purpose of improving
clinical care.
And the office does that through different means.
First, we engage with academic institutions ensuring the
coordination between NSW Health and universities or

research centres. We also administer various grant
programs, so we allocate funding to medical research
institutes, we allocate funding that is targeted at
specific areas of research, so grants in cardiovascular
diseases, for example, or in spinal cord injury, and we
also work on supporting the governance of research in the
healthcare system, and that means establishing more
standardised ways to manage ethics, confidentiality
assurance, that relates to the management of research.
And finally we work in partnerships with either
academic institutions, local health districts research
teams or industry, at working on the infrastructure that is
required to make specific areas of research more conducive
to impacts on the healthcare system. These are the main
functions of OHMR and how it, you know, again tries to make
research part of the delivery of health care in New South
Wales.
Q. So if we just look at paragraph 14 now, it says that
there is a budget of 104.7 million for that, and that's
this year's budget. Would that be a typical budget for
OHMR or have there been any significant changes in recent
years?
A. No, there's not been significant changes, but year on
year it will be slightly different, depending on the timing
of specific grant programs. So with certain grant programs
finishing, some years we could have a reduction, and of
course there are always new grants coming in. So there is
a bit of fluctuation in the overall budget but over the
last few years it's been fairly stable.
Q. So looking just for this year, then, it says at 14b
that 44.5 million, which by my calculation is about
42.5 per cent of the total budget, has been allocated to
the day-to-day costs of running independent medical
research institutes. How is the effectiveness of that
spend evaluated?
A. There are various ways that we evaluate the impact of
our investments within the Office for Health and Medical
Research. First, we have a small team that is dedicated to
monitoring and evaluation of programs, and we do have to
report, depending on the source of funding, on the
achievements related to our grant funding.
We do also monitor different indicators of
performance, either with regards to the timeliness of

ethics reviews or governance approvals, and we do receive
reports from the different groups that receive funding from
the office as part of that work.
Another area is that we have worked with various
academic institutions in progressing stronger frameworks to
assess impacts. Traditionally, impacts of health research
was mostly calculated in terms of number of publications or
the grants that those institutions would receive from
national funding, for example, but increasingly we're also
asking them to reflect on the impact that it has on local
policies or specific delivery programs in health care so
that we can have a more rounded approach.
As part of the medical research support program that
you're talking about, we do have specific metrics that we
revise with them that relates to their academic
achievements, and that is also integrated in the review
of the level of funding that they receive on an ongoing
basis, and there have been shifts according to, you know,
the performance of those organisations in the more than
10 years that the program has been in place.
Q. Now, given that some of these medical research
institutes would be operating in the same space, doing
research in similar sorts of conditions, how do you avoid
duplication of the way that the money is being distributed,
particularly if they're competing for research grants that
are the same source, et cetera?
A. So in the case of the medical research institute and
the medical research support program, this is
infrastructure funding. So it's not funding that we give
for specific research activities, it's really to support
them as organisations so that they can be functioning in an
efficient way, an effective way, and it's for their
researchers to actually determine what are the programs
that they will apply to receive operating expenditure as
part of grant programs.
We do have conversations with the entire sector, we
meet with the various associations, including the
Association of Medical Research Institutes that we have in
New South Wales, on a regular basis, and therefore, at
times we do provide advice if we feel that there are
certain areas where, you know, there's opportunities for
new research to be conducted. But again, the funding that
we give is not tied to that; it's really infrastructure

funding, helping them to exist as centres.
Q. If we go to paragraph 14c, that's about medical
technology and commercialisation initiatives. Can you tell
us a bit more about that?
A. Yes. So the Medical Devices Fund is a fund that was
established around 10 years ago. It's a fund that aims at
helping start-ups and other companies or clinicians that
have great ideas in terms of how medical technologies can
actually help to deliver care in a different way, to
accelerate their projects.
So what we do in that program is we give grants on
a competitive basis, so we have independent committees
assessing the proposals, and the most promising medical
devices are selected for funding and that enables them to
do the work that they need to at times bring those medical
devices to a commercialisation stage, which means that they
can then start to sell these medical devices on the market.
We select only a few of the, you know, all of the
proposals that we receive, and we provide them with support
in different ways to make sure that we increase their
capabilities for commercialisation. Many of those devices
are created by clinicians working in our system and,
therefore, we need to help them to better understand how do
you manage intellectual property, how do you engage with
people that can potentially provide funding, how do you
advertise and promote your medical device for it to be
a successful endeavour?
That's what the commercialisation training program
does and the Brandon BioCatalyst collaboration does as
well. Those two structures are enabling us to provide
a wrap around the programs so that we ensure that we're not
just investing money to help those medical devices to be
successful, we're also providing them the support so that
they can really truly accelerate their development and
ensure their success.
Q. You mentioned Brandon BioCatalyst. Can you tell us
what that is exactly and what is its role?
A. Brandon BioCatalyst is an Australian venture capital
fund and in our case, they participate in the
commercialisation training program to give advice to the
medical device fund trainees about the best way to engage
with funders, so that they can bring their innovations to

the next stage of funding. The Medical Devices Fund is
really just an acceleration fund. At some point, some of
those companies are at a stage where they need to produce
at a larger scale and that's the advice that they - you
know, that's the advice that Brandon BioCatalyst provides
within our context.
Q. And when you say the most promising of the very many
proposals that you receive are the ones that are supported,
is that the most promising in the sense of being
commercially successful or addressing patient problems or
having the most impact on patient outcomes? What's the
measure?
A. It's both of those things, and the committees that
evaluate the candidates every year have specific criteria
that they use to assess them, and it includes the stage of
development of those medical devices, so have they already
demonstrated that, you know, it can work? It includes the
potential impact on patients and on the healthcare system,
because sometimes those medical devices will help to
deliver more care for patients or deliver technologies that
are enhancing the current treatments that we have for
patients; but it's also with regards to their economic
potential. This is really about ensuring that our clinical
entrepreneurs can be supported.
So all of those different aspects are part of the
decisions. This is not something that I control. We've
got peer review groups that do that in an independent way
and then recommend to the program which candidates should
be supported.
Q. Can you give us some examples of particular devices or
initiatives that have been commercialised in this way after
being developed by people working in the system?
A. There are many examples, given the fact that we've
supported more than 40, if I remember, different devices
through the years - or, sorry, 80 different medical
devices. Some of them relate to very clinical areas, such
as finding ways to provide dialysis in a different way.
There are some that relate to digital applications,
for example, or at least providing a digital application
support on a specific device. In terms of specific
examples, if you'd just allow me - I think I have mentioned
some, but at the moment they're escaping me in terms of
those that have reached commercialisation stage. I can

find that for you a bit later.
Q. That's okay. Does the OHMR monitor to see whether
they do have the anticipated benefits for patients or
commercial success?
A. There are various - again, there are multiple
modalities we can do to monitor that, depending on the
specific device or specific grant programs that OHMR
supports. There are - in some of those programs, we have
evaluation programs, independent evaluations, that need to
be provided, and we do them at regular intervals to make
sure that we provide an input back into the system and we
provide the right adjustment to increase effectiveness.
So, for example --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. So something that doesn't work
very well for patients is unlikely to have much prospects
for commercial success; right?
A. That is correct. If something doesn't generate the
outcomes for patients, it's very unlikely that people will
want to purchase those medical devices, and in a similar
fashion for other grants that we have, if a research study
doesn't demonstrate an impact, then it's not something we
would promote for implementation at scale afterwards.
So there are things that relate to every single
project's evaluation, as well as an evaluation of the
entire programs that we put in place, and I was about to
say that the translation research grant programs, for
example, was evaluated after its second year and that
allowed us to make adjustment to the program to ensure that
the projects we are supporting, you know, we assess them
with the right criteria to ensure that they're going to be
successful.
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. In paragraph 14d there, there is
a reference to the Translational Research Grants Scheme,
and that is for projects that have the potential to benefit
patients quickly. Can you give us some examples of
successes in terms of those TRGS grants?
A. Yes. So there's been many programs. We're at our
eighth round of translational research grant programs now.
One example is the monitoring of electrocardiograms, so
that's to assess the heart, you know, electrical rate.
That was developed in Hunter New England. It was part of
the translational research grant programs and demonstrated
really that we could have a more streamlined access to

quick diagnostics for cardiac care for patients living in
rural settings, and the program is currently being
implemented across the entire Hunter New England region and
we're monitoring it on an ongoing basis to see the
potential for other areas as well. So it's a good example
of a program that went to the translational research
grants, that demonstrated, you know, a really good impact
on the system.
Q. Are there programs that have been - or projects that
been funded by these grants that have been rolled out
across the state?
A. Yes. For example, the naloxone program is one that
went through the translational research grant to evaluate
the impact of accessing that drug at home on the health of
patients, and following very positive pilots funded through
the translational research grant program, it has been
rolled out across the entire state and is now used across
many drug and alcohol centres as a way to treat patients in
a standard way.
Q. Now, the TRGS funds, as I understand it - that
$5 million is entirely money from the state; is that
correct?
A. That's correct.
Q. And when you were speaking previously about the types
of grants that the medical research institutes could apply
for, were they only state grants or are there other sources
of those?
A. No, I was talking about other sources of funding such
as the National Health and Medical Research Council, but
also the MRFF, which is another Commonwealth-led program,
and of course, there are also funding that they receive
through philanthropy or specific funding sources that may
be provided by clinical patient programs, you know.
There's a few sources of funding, although the main sources
of funding for those medical research institutes are the
NHMRC and the MRFF in volume.
Q. So of that 104.7 million budget for OHMR, is that
entirely state funding?
A. That's entirely state funding.
Q. And just finishing on the TRGS, have there been
learnings from projects that were funded but were deemed
not to be successful?

A. Well, yes. There's been various learning as part.
TRGS program in general. What we can say from our
evaluation is that 40 per cent of programs that went
through - projects that went through the program have
demonstrated successes and have been implemented at the
state level. 30 per cent usually demonstrate a potential
effectiveness but still need a bit of work to really
understand or to help us assess if we need to roll those
programs across the entire state. And there is 30 per cent
of projects that didn't demonstrate enough effectiveness.
And that's the goal of the program, you know, we
wouldn't expect 100 per cent of projects to demonstrate
that they would be effective. The goal of the program is
to actually trial interesting ideas coming out of the
system and really assess if they work before we invest
further in implementing them statewide.
There are some learnings that came out of the
evaluation as well with regards to the fact for those
projects to have a very strong endorsement locally from
their chief executives that are promoting them in their
districts. They need to have a very clear measurement
approach. They need to be mobilising clinicians locally so
that they get implemented, and all of those are the types
of learning that we have made through the years and now we
help projects before they arrive to reflect on those
different aspects and they're part of the things that we
assess with the peer review committees to decide which ones
will receive funding going forward. So the evaluation we
did of the program did enable us to reflect on some
learnings and then integrate them into the later rounds of
the program.
Q. We might just move down to paragraph 14e, at the top
of the page there. So you refer there to 15 million, this
year, at least, being spent on cardiovascular research
capacity. Can you give us a bit more detail of what that
covers?
A. Yes. So that fund is a fund that we have for
10 years, we're about midway through it. The goal was to
lift our competitiveness nationally and internationally in
research grants in cardiovascular research. What it covers
are various types of grants, first, early and mid-career
grants, really helping young researchers to better
establish their career, have a stronger lab platform to
then be competitive and receive funding from national

organisations.
It includes funds that we use to attract emerging
researchers internationally that we feel would provide
something back to New South Wales, which would be a good
new asset in cardiovascular research. And then it also
provides funding for specific projects.
I want to, for example, mention the fact that we will
have a targeted call for proposals about cardiovascular
health for Aboriginal people this year, and that's a way
for us to at times target the funding in an area where we
think we need to lift, we need to increase capability in a
more targeted way.
Q. And then if we look at paragraph g, omics research and
omics technologies, it sounds like a space-age word but can
you please explain to the Commissioner and the group what
this actually means and what it involves?
A. Of course. "Omics" is a term, a very generic term
that is there to describe many different things, and
probably the most known area is genomics, which is the
science of genes and the science of intervening to modify
genetic illnesses to improve the health of patients.
So our omics work doesn't just cover genomics, it
does, but it covers proteomics, which is about the science
of proteins in the body so unfortunately it is a bit, you
know, cutting edge and complex, but ultimately, if I am to
summarise our work in that space, it is that we're really
working with our partners to make sure that all of the
promises of personalised medicine, which is really medicine
that is about the specific genetics of people, the specific
genomics of cancers that they may get, et cetera, so that
the real personalisation of our treatments can be supported
and be embedded into our system. And therefore, it's about
that translation of cutting-edge, you know, benchtop
research happening in universities and research centres,
and helping them along the way so that we transform it into
clinical applications at the bedside for patients. That's
really our omics work.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Are they who you're referring to
when you say "our partners"?
A. The partners in that omics space would be
universities.

Q. And the research institutes?
A. Research institutes, but at times it could be
industry, if specific industries are developing
technologies that we feel are at the stage where we can
start to support their implementation in clinical settings.
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. Can we scroll, please, to
paragraph 15. Now, it refers there to OHMR's annual
priorities and work plan deliverables being negotiated and
recommended by the branch's executive team. Does this
involve any consultation with the local health districts
about the needs of their populations and their challenges
and what they're doing to address them on the ground?
A. Yes. And there are various ways that we achieve this.
First, there are regular structures that enable us to have
close connections with the local districts' chief
executives, such as the senior executive forum, where the
Office for Health and Medical Research and the ACI are
presenting their planned work, receive feedback about their
adjustment with regards to local needs or feedback about
things that we may need to adjust to better fit the
clinical setting. And that's, of course, really also
enabling each of the local districts to get a better
understanding and an early view about the type of work that
the Office for Health and Medical Research and ACI are
progressing.
We also have two communities of practice that enable
us to better connect locally as well, both in terms of
research as well as innovation. So we've got a community
of practice which is a group of people having to achieve
similar kind of work, and it's called the community of
practice of directors of research, and they are the
directors of research that are active at the local district
level, working with their research teams at identifying
specific opportunities, specific needs. And they now meet
on a monthly basis to reflect about their specific needs
but also the things we need to do at the state level to
support their work, which, of course, is a very important
role of the Office for Health and Medical Research.
And we also have a community of practice of directors
of innovation. They don't always have that name, but we
know who is leading, you know, innovation and translation
work in the district, and they also meet on a monthly basis
to reflect on our implementation programs, you know, the
things that we're bringing at scale at the moment.

There's also, of course, at times consultation with
the districts and specific hospitals or research centres
that we do as part of specific programs. So, for example,
when we do an evaluation or when we want to reorient
specific programs, we would very often organise
a consultation where people will be able to reflect on the
previous program and identify potential gaps that we need

Hasn't the ACI got more of a responsibility than merely
discouraging people from doing procedures when there is, as
you say, no clinical benefit to the patient?

models of care and our clinical practice guides when
a procedure shouldn't be performed anymore or if
a procedure is still, you know, not just recommended but
should be part of standards of care and therefore be
offered to patients systematically.
What that specific sentence and program reflects on is
the fact that, for some procedures, it's not the procedure
on its own that should never be done; the reality is that
it should be done for specific patients with specific
clinical indication. That's where we say we need to
encourage and work with clinicians so that we reduce the
number of patients that may receive a back surgery or
a knee surgery whilst they didn't have all of the clinical
criteria that would make them a likely patient that would
benefit from that surgery.
The reality is that in many clinical areas, it's a bit

assess certain types of surgery, they may say 50 per cent
of patients received surgery and did not benefit from it.

from being effective for that patient. That's why, in our

"You need to have a multidisciplinary team discussion in

that patient will benefit from surgery."

know, encouraging and convincing the system, because we
know that ultimately, at the end of the day, for those
procedures, it's the clinical team and the patients that
will have to make the decision. It's not the role of ACI
to govern that, you know? But ACI, of course, when
a procedure is no longer perceived as being the gold
standard, we have the responsibility to make it clear in
our models of care and our clinical practice guide.

really is in those areas where it's more of a fit between

the patient and the procedure, where we need to work with
clinical practices more in a collaborative way and it
cannot be prescriptive, you know, to reduce that low-value
care.

directors of surgery, many directors of anaesthesia, from
the different districts, we can really connect across the
entire state.
Q. One of the procedures - we don't need to go to this

a procedure done by ENT surgeons; is that correct?

Q. So there may be some districts, smaller districts,

I can see you nodding in that regard. So that is correct,

A. Yes.
Q. That does these procedures?
A. Yes. In some distribution there may be only one ENT

rotate to cover the needs of surgery in those districts.
Q. So how would a district put in place a governance

A. Yeah. So that's something that we would work with the

program, not just comprised of specific surgeons but,
instead, also mobilising paediatricians, if we're talking
about grommets, it could be something useful, just so that
it's not just based on a single surgeon's decision,
socialised with a group through a rigorous process, so that
various types of clinicians can provide an input.
So we wouldn't expect all of those to be done within
each of the surgical specialties, anyway, and if there's
any support to give to some of those regional areas, that's
something we would explore from the ACI perspective, but it
would be only to facilitate the process, again, not to make

THE COMMISSIONER: Q. How long has spinal fusion for

A. My apologies; I didn't get your question.
Q. How long has spinal fusion for back pain alone not

A. It's not really time based. It's really one of those

Q. We're straying, but just that when I started a lawyer
which is a long time ago, every single plaintiff with a bad

back had spinal fusion surgery.
A. Sorry, I didn't quite get your question. So do you

Q. Yes.

THE COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. Could we just move to paragraph 58 of
the statement, please. So this is about reducing clinical
variation, sometimes called unwarranted clinical practice
variation. So it's said that this is an area of strategic
importance for the ACI. Can you just explain in a bit more
detail what this is?
A. Yes. So what we call unwarranted clinical variation
is variation in care that patients are receiving that we
cannot put - or that cannot be explained by variation in
patients' needs or preferences for care, okay? So
patients can, you know, have specific needs, but, of course
some patients may not want a surgery, for example, or some
patients may not want certain types of cancer treatment.
And there are procedures where we can see that the care
that's provided to patients does vary, and it doesn't
correlate with variation in needs or evidence that it's the
expectations of patients that are different.
That variation can be in terms of the actual
procedures that are offered to patients or the way those
procedures are performed, you know, laparoscopically or
through open surgery or done in hospital versus through
support at home. There are various ways to look at
variation to reflect on that.
What's unwarranted really is where, you know, for
example, we may think that in a certain region they've got
more of a certain type of procedure and it's not because
they've got more patients with an indication for that
procedure, okay? So that's unwarranted clinical variation.
Q. And when you identify an example of unwarranted
clinical variation, do you find resistance to changing
practice?
A. There's very often resistance to change, either
because clinicians are not aware that the evidence in the

literature has changed and, therefore, their practice needs
to change, or because, you know, the change management
required to support them to provide care in a different way
is significant. You know, clinicians may not want to
change the way they deliver care if they're not supported
in the right way through outpatient support and all of
those things. But it could also be resistance because
patients need to also be informed about the fact that the
standards of care are changing.
It is well known in the literature that, you know,
following a demonstration of evidence that a certain
practice is not a good practice anymore or that a new
practice needs to be adopted, there's ample evidence that
suggests that it takes time, it takes a few years before
clinicians will adopt it, and there are pockets of
clinicians that do not change their practices on the longer
term. That's why agencies like the ACI and the Clinical
Excellence Commission, for example, exist - because we're
there to support that process, engage with clinicians, make
sure that they're aware that the standards of care have
changed, mobilise their clinicians so that they're informed
about it, and also at the right times find the right
champions that will say publicly, "It's time for us to
change the way we deliver care for patients", you know, and
we use different levers to try to address the clinical
variation. But, you know, spontaneously, we know that it
takes effort to support adoption of those new practices
across complex healthcare systems like NSW Health.
Q. Is it sometimes the case that there could be a vested
interest in maintaining the status quo even when the
practitioner is presented with the evidence that it's no
longer good practice?
A. There has been studies that have demonstrated that
sometimes, financial or, you know, regulatory interest come
in the way, and that means that we need to work at
identifying those potential barriers and make sure that we
adjust funding models and regulatory approaches so that we,
you know, make it easier for clinicians to adopt those when
it is known that it could have a financial impact or an
impact on medicolegal issues, which, of course, are very
legitimate things to consider when we want to promote
adoption at the system level.
Q. And that's a role for the ACI, to be involved in some
of those changes?

A. The role of ACI is really to identify when such levers
will either become a barrier or would facilitate adoption,
and work with our partners within the ministry or with
other pillars or with the local districts so that we make
the right adjustments and really making sure that we
facilitate adoption by clinicians. But it's not for the
ACI to make all of those changes, given the fact that we're
an advisory body much more than a body that, you know,
governs and manages the system.
Q. Understood. So what actions is the ACI taking in
relation to unwarranted clinical variation currently?
A. So, of course, we've got 42 different clinical
networks, many of them do have a reflection on clinical
variation at the moment, and we produce, again, clinical
practice guides that really clarify to clinicians what is
the current standard of practice. We develop tools so that
local clinicians can start to work with their peers to
identify where there's clinical variation and start to
address it, and we're currently also designing a more
systematic program of measurement and action to cut across
the different specialties to more effectively continue to
address clinical variation.
The reality is that the ACI has worked on clinical
variation since its inception. Now, we're at the stage
where we can formalise and systematise a lot of that work
and prioritise in areas where there will be a stronger
benefit, and we're currently restructuring our clinical
variation work through a clinical variation action plan
that we have endorsed again before the pandemic, and
therefore we had to be cognisant of the fact that clinical
settings were disrupted at that time. But now that we're
getting to a different phase, with many clinical settings,
you know, back to where they were, it's time for us to
re-instigate that work, and that's part of our priorities
for the next few financial years.
Q. Would there be scope sometimes for, say, a slightly
more interventional role in the sense that you might have
a policy that requires clinicians to inform patients about
new evidence that - in relation to a procedure they're
recommending?
A. We already do that through our clinical guidance when
there is already a shared decision-making process. We're
already suggesting to clinicians that they use the tools
that we have provided so that they are more systematically,

you know, touching on the key points. We've not mandated
it. However, in some clinical areas, there could be
a mandate for some of those tools.
It's the same with clinical checklists. We can
identify when we feel clinicians need to more
systematically go through specific criteria but again they
are not mandated at the moment as part of our work. We
would only propose to the ministry to do that when there's
absolute evidence that this is now standard of care to the
level where every single patient should go through it, and
at times, when we support the review of policies, we do
propose for those tools to be referred directly in the
policy.
Q. We might move to "Technical and Clinical Innovation",
which is your next section, so if we can just scroll down,
I think it is probably the next page. There we go, just
there - or maybe if we go to, sorry, paragraph 64. You've
described there some advanced therapeutics that ACI has
been involved with or OHMR has been involved with, and they
look like very interesting innovations obviously. Can you
tell us about the bacteriophage or "phage" therapy, and in
particular the clinical implications for this?
A. Yes, so bacteriophages viruses that are harmless to
humans that we know are harmful for bacterias. So that's
the concept. So some viruses do attack bacterias,
bacterias are a bigger organism compared to viruses. In
nature, we find a lot of viruses that are actually keeping
in check some of those bacterias. Therefore, phage therapy
is really the clinical application of that concept, where
we can use some viruses that we know will not harm patients
but will target some of the chronic infections that they
have.
The purpose is for us to create a system where we can
more systematically identify the bacterias, their
susceptibilities, and find in our bank of viruses some that
would enable to target a treatment to those bacterias.
It's mostly used as an adjuvant to usual care, so by
"adjuvant", I mean as a, you know, a complementary kind of
therapy, and it's mostly used in cases where patients have
got intractable infections that are not responding to
antibiotics anymore or have bacterias that are
multiresistant to all of our antibiotics, and there's been
cases treated where we cured them of those chronic

infections because we've found the right virus that can
then target those infections and kill them in the body, and
afterwards, all of those viruses are, you know, also
expelled from the body by the immune system.
So that's what we are doing. It's an emerging
science, and we're working very closely with the scientific
team at Westmead to progress that, but also progress
a model where it can be made accessible and available more
broadly across the system, and that's what our advanced
therapeutics team is working on at the moment, really
partnering around the science but also the delivery
component of it, just so that we can really harness the
benefits for our patients.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Just on that, so at the start of
64 you've said that the Office for Health and Medical
Research advanced therapeutics team supports the
development and delivery of, in this case we're talking
about bacteriophage - or "phaige"?
A. I think it's either said as phage or "phaiges" in the
literature, so --
Q. I'll probably use both. Just if you want to, could
you just - sorry if you haven't given a complete answer,
the way the OHMR supports the development of this
particular therapy, is there anything further you want to
point out in terms of what the OHMR does?
A. Well, what the office does, when we find a new area
where there's obviously emerging evidence about a new
treatment that will come and we could use, the first thing
we do is that we assess what's the current capability of
the system to actually integrate that new therapy into the
system; is there further research that we need to do in
support; is there some infrastructure that we need to put
in place?
In the case of phage therapy, for example, we know we
need a biobank to be able to deliver that as a service, and
by "biobank", I really mean a place where we will have
different viruses, different types of viruses available
then to be manufactured and produced, to be able to be
given to a patient. If we don't have that bank of virus,
then it's unlikely we're going to find a specific bacteria
in a patient that could be treated by that. And of course,
it's the role of OHMR to work with the system at
identifying, you know, do we need to work with regulatory

agencies to make sure that we can produce those new
therapies in a way that meets the TGA, for example?
We work sometimes with pathology and other groups to
make sure that we could bank those new therapeutics. We
work with local districts when they say that their staff
are not trained to be able to manipulate some of those new
therapies as well. So we've got programs in pharmacology,
for example, that aim at lifting that capability of the
system. That's where you can see that the Office for
Health and Medical Research has got mandates that relate to
the proximal part of research, you know, really making sure
that we accelerate research so that it translates into
useable products, and then the ACI can take the relay and
work with the clinical systems to embed them after. And
again, at some point, phage therapy is probably one where
some networks of ACI will start to work on models of care,
for example.
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. Just one other question about the
phage therapy, is it fair to say that that's part of the
answer, scientifically, to the problems we see with
antibiotic resistance in the community?
A. It's one of the tools that we have. Of course, we
need to make sure we use antibiotics in an appropriate way,
and we've got a lot of clinical models that do cover that,
and the CEC, of course, have got a very important role in
drug management. But this one is helping us - when things
start, unfortunately for the patient, to be really
difficult to manage, you know, we've got some patients that
we've treated that spend weeks in hospital because of those
chronic infections, this is an additional tool we can use
and offer clinicians so that they can resolve those
multiresistance issues.
Q. If we just scroll down to the second example, 64b, so
this is gene therapy, and in particular, viral vector
delivery technology. Can you just outline what OHMR's role
has been in that and what promise it holds?
A. Okay. So gene therapy is a very broad term that
means, you know, using fragments of genes and replacing
those fragments of genes into, you know, cells in different
organs to make those organs or biological systems, you
know, start to produce the protein that, from a genetic
perspective, they are not producing, or stop producing some
of those proteins that are creating illnesses. And viral
vector is a specific technology that enables the

transportation of those gene therapies into the appropriate
cell.
So let me just explain, a viral vector is again
a virus that is innocuous or harmless for humans, that we
use as a way to deliver a gene therapy to a specific organ.
And what we do, or what the researchers and the academic
teams do, is that they find ways to identify and package
viruses so that they will respond to a specific receptor on
specific cells, so that, a bit like a mailbox system, they
will deliver the gene therapy in the right place, okay?
We've all heard of the, you know, SARS-CoV2 virus and
the way it was linking to the spike protein, you know,
well, in a similar fashion, the adenoviruses and the
lentiviruses that we use in viral vector therapy identify
a specific protein on the surface of cells, and then they
get into the cell and they exchange the faulty gene for
a good gene and then that cell starts to produce the right
protein, okay? So that's, in a nutshell, the technology
that we're talking about.
It's not the only one to give genetic therapies, but
it is one that, in New South Wales, we knew we had
expertise and we had teams that were able to potentially
bring this not just in the research space but actually in
the clinical space, so that we would start to treat
patients and potentially even turn this into
a commercialisation endeavour.
The role of OHMR has been to work with the system at
identifying what were their needs in terms of the research
they needed to do to bring that technology to fruition,
work again with regulatory organisations so that we would
be able to bring the system to be able to manufacture those
new therapies in a way that would fit with the TGA, for
example, and also identify how would we start to produce
this in a way that commercially would make sense and in a
way that would also enable our system to access that
technology at a lower price, because obviously you can
purchase those technologies internationally at the moment,
they are extremely expensive treatment.
So the role of OHMR is to work with the system so that
we work on those different aspects, making sure it happens.
Of course, we never produce the actual treatment, that's
all done at the local level, with the research institutes,

but it's about being the catalyst of that change so that it
happens. Many research teams come to us and say, "We need
a bit of help on this aspect", or, "We need you to help us
with our intellectual property", or, "We need you to help
us in terms of training of some staff", for example. In
viral vector, we did all of those things through the last
few years so that we'd bring that manufacturing capacity to
New South Wales.
Q. Is New South Wales leading the way, in terms of the
nation, that is, in regard to these two, the gene therapy
and the bacteriophage therapy?
A. In many respects, yes. In terms of viral vector, we
have announced yesterday, actually, the creation of
a company that will lead the manufacture of viral vectors,
and it's the only such facility that will exist in
Australia, and in many aspects of gene therapies we have,
you know, world-leading teams, really, in certain areas.
But gene therapy is such a broad area. There are, of
course, pockets of excellence all over the place, but
New South Wales is really well positioned overall in
precision medicine, you know, and gene therapy and our
capability in that space, in the kids' gene therapy
treatment as well as increasingly in adults, is really
a strength that we can build on.
Q. Does that open the door perhaps for collaborations
with other states to be able to roll out innovations from
New South Wales?
A. Absolutely. And OHMR has in the past established
networks that contributed to the national scene so that we
would mobilise not just the experts and the leaders that we
have in New South Wales but the broader group or community
of academics that are working in a specific area, and
I would say that for phage it's a good example because we
have supporting the academic team to start a national
network of specialists in phage therapy, again making sure
that we collaborate and coordinate across states.
Q. Just moving down to an example of the technical
innovation, and you've talked there about virtual care, we
touched on that before, can you maybe just briefly outline
the advances that have been made in the last three years in
relation to virtual care?
A. Yes. So there's been obviously a really increased
rate of adoption of virtual technologies in NSW Health.

The fact that, you know, through the pandemic we were not
able to bring many patients to physical outpatient clinics
for the purpose of managing the pandemic has already
contributed to that. It has helped clinicians also to see
how they can use those technologies as part of routine
care, and we can see now we have higher adoption rates of
virtual modalities to treat patients, compared to prior to
the pandemic.
There's been advances in terms of the tools that we
have in New South Wales, so we've got a platform called
myVirtualCare, it's one of the platforms that is used to
treat patients on an outpatient basis or after they're
discharged from hospital, so that clinicians and patients
can have a joint consultation without patients having to
come physically to the clinic or to the hospital, and of
course, in rural settings, that means, you know, hundreds
or thousands of kilometres saved for those patients.
There's been advances in terms of what is known in the
literature as virtual wards, which really means - or
virtual hospital, where many of the functions that we do
for patients admitted to hospital can now be done at home,
if we deliver to the patients the right technology so that
they can be followed centrally from the hospital but by
remaining at home, and, you know, RPA Virtual is a good
example of that being progressed in New South Wales.
Of course, Telestroke is an example that I've given,
and it is a virtual care platform because the clinicians
that treat patients for stroke in the hub do receive all of
the imaging done locally through that virtual system so
that they can interpret directly all of the imaging for
patients.
So there are different modalities that we've
progressed. And I will just conclude by the example of
HOPE again, the health outcomes and patient experience.
It's a different type of virtual care. It's what we call
asynchronous virtual care, so it is virtual care that it is
not - where patients and clinicians are not looking at the
same thing at the same time, but ultimately it's virtual
care because it enables clinicians to see from their
patients if they're not doing well and if they need to be
contacted, without having the patients needing to come in,
in the clinical office, or the emergency department, and
therefore it is providing a virtual modality to provide and

deliver that care. So I just wanted to provide a few
examples of the things that have really progressed within
NSW Health.
Q. And HOPE is about patient experience as well as
patient outcomes; is that correct?
A. Yes, that's correct, and by "patient outcomes", we
really main their symptoms, their quality of life, you
know, the things that they would express if they were to
come to a clinic, you know, to say, "I'm not doing fine",
so we're talking about pain, we're talking about sleep,
we're talking about their ability to move around, you know,
things that relate to their quality of life, but it is also
about their experience. And by "experience" we mean, you
know, do they feel that care was provided in a way that
promoted good continuity or did they have to repeat the
same information at every visit, for example? Do they feel
that they've got enough information to take care of their
problem when they go back home? So the platform covers
really both aspects.
Q. Let's move to paragraph 66. This is now talking about
identifying, assessing, developing and implementing
innovations. In 66a there you talk about the critical
intelligence unit. So can you perhaps just start by
discussing exactly what that is?
A. Yes. So the critical intelligence unit is a small
team that we have established during the COVID pandemic, so
it started as the COVID-19 critical intelligence unit, and
it's basically a small unit that has the mandate to provide
extremely rapid review of evidence to support
decision-making at the right time, you know, supporting
myself, supporting other decision-makers in the system,
ahead of specific meetings or ahead of specific decisions
that they had to make, very often during the pandemic on
a daily basis, as you can imagine, and making sure that we
were always going back to the literature and assessing how
knowledge was evolving.
Of course, during the COVID pandemic, you know,
a month away really meant that, at times, what we thought
we knew was completely changed, and that's why a critical
intelligence unit was required. We needed a dedicated team
that had the time to track the progression of the evidence
and provide, you know, independent advice to support
decision-making.

It was a highly successful model, you know, and
therefore, we were asked to keep this going, both for the
purpose of continuing to support clinical decision and
policy decision in New South Wales with that capacity to
review rapidly the literature and provide scientific
advice, but also as a way to be prepared if we got another
pandemic or a recrudescence of COVID-19. So it was part
of, you know, making sure we would keep an infrastructure
that had demonstrated that it could benefit the system.
Q. About just over half way down that paragraph, after
the brackets, it says:
Publications that describe innovations in
clinical care in [New South Wales] are
compiled into an Evidence Digest ...
Why is it limited to innovations and clinical care in
New South Wales?
A. Actually, it's not the right way to describe it. This
is the evidence that's coming internationally, but the
process is that within New South Wales we want to reach
clinicians from our system to inform them about that
international evidence. So it is absolutely about all of
those international academic journals, it's about the
international organisations that are providing advice as
well, and the critical intelligence unit provides the
weekly evidence digest, looking at all of those sources of
information. So it's not just - it's not just about the
innovations within New South Wales.
Q. I thought that might be the case but I wanted to
clarify.
A. Thank you for that.
Q. So it says that it goes out to 1100 subscribers.
Would you agree that this is actually a very small number
relative to the size of the workforce in NSW Health?
A. We obviously want to increase the number of
subscribers to the evidence digest. It is increasing on
a month-by-month basis. It is used - the subscribers are
70 per cent clinicians and 30 per cent are people that say
they've got a policy role in the system or more of
a managerial role in the system. We don't know if those
70 per cent of clinicians, you know, are they all the ones
that are organising care in New South Wales? We don't know
that. But we will certainly continue to publicise the

existence of the evidence digest so that we increase the
number of subscribers, but in just a few months of
operation, it is still quite a good reach. But we're
continuing to advertise it.
Q. So I appreciate it's too early to have been evaluated
as yet, but is there any sort of plan to look at whether
these evidence digests are actually translating into
decision-making on that basis of what the evidence is?
A. Yes, and what we do is that we do track the specific
papers that are open or accessed through the digest on an
ongoing basis, so we can see the reach, which type of paper
seems to have, you know, got interest from clinicians, and
the digest is not just used by the people receiving it
through our electronic mailing system; it's also used by
different teams that are currently developing and designing
models of care.
So we do have other processes where we discuss the
digest with specific clinical groups and therefore we
already have evidence of elements of the digest that were
picked up and integrated into new models of care, because
it's part of the evidence review tools that we have.
Q. Is there a requirement for policymakers to refer to
these evidence digests and align their policies to them?
A. No, there's no requirement. This is really provided
for the sake of disseminating that evidence. We do have
other tools that synthesise the evidence in specific areas
that we produce - evidence checks, et cetera - and very
often we're asked to produce them for policymakers at the
time of their review.
Q. So is there any way in place that you can manage
inconsistency in terms of some of the policies coming out,
relative to the evidence, that they may not be informed by?
A. There's currently no mandatory processes in place for
that to happen. What is happening at the moment is that,
you know, we receive requests from all of the different
branches of the ministry and many pillars and local
districts. When they are revising policies, then they ask
us to provide that kind of evidence support.
Q. So on the next line, it refers to this digest
subsequently being reviewed by a clinical panel to identify
potential game changers. What happens when they identify
such a game changer?

A. Yes, so just before I answer that, I just want to say
that a game changer for us is really an advance in clinical
practice demonstrated by the research that we feel will
change clinical care or will change clinical delivery of
care. So when our clinical panel reviews the digest and
identifies that there's really a breakthrough in the
literature, what we do is that we would either go to
a specific clinical network to discuss this and see how we
can translate that into an existing tool or if we need to
develop a new instrument, but also at times we will surface
it to our colleagues within the ministry when we feel that
it relates to a program of work that, you know, they're
working on, either in sustainability in health care or
virtual care or any different aspect.
So the ACI takes responsibility then of having
discussions with the appropriate group about what is the
best next step in terms of progressing that game changer.
It could still be that we need to wait for more
evidence to accumulate before we're convinced we need to
build a pilot, you know, or test some of those, or it could
be that the game changer is actually helping us to inform
the next iteration of a current program, and again, we
bring it to different platforms including the future health
steering committees when required.
Q. And at what point would the system - the health
services - be made aware that there may be something of
this nature on the horizon?
A. I would say that it's still variable because we're
really bedding this process at the moment, trialling to see
what's the best way to identify and then progress game
changers. We need to be cognisant of funding cycles. We
need to be cognisant of the fact that for some of those
game changers, there's a lot of things that we will have to
adapt or adjust before we can actually roll them out, and
therefore, we need to also adapt it to the specific areas
that it relates to.
You know, as you know, it takes longer time to train
people differently if a game changer is about using
a different type of professional to deliver a certain
service, or it takes time to adjust models of care if
a game changer is more about specific aspects of the
standards of care. So it will have to be variable, but
again we're learning to work with that system. We think

that the advance that we've made is to really make it
systematic, that we go through the literature and have
a mechanic in place to surface what's promising.
Q. Who's on the clinical panel that looks at these?
A. So there's two clinical panels that we can use,
depending on the game changer. The first one is the Health
System Advisory Council, and the membership of the council
is available on the website. You know, it's a broad group
of clinical leaders across the system and managers that
have leadership roles as well, and it is covers a broad
range of clinical areas. So I won't - you know, I wouldn't
be able to name all of the members of the group. But we

collaborative and the national surgical quality improvement
program, or NSQIP. Have these resulted in changes being
embedded into practice across New South Wales?
A. Yes. Absolutely. So if we look at the paediatric
improvement collaborative, for example, it really enabled
us to avoid duplicating standards of care and models of
care that were already produced by one of the lead
institutions in paediatrics in the country, which is the
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne.
Clinicians told us that the guidelines that they used
come from the Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. So what
we did is we collaborated with Queensland, Victoria and
New South Wales to structure a joint approach where we
would have one single way to produce those clinical guides
and then we would promote their adoptions in the three
states, and in this way, we can mobilise, you know, our
limited funding to other clinical areas.
We know that those guidelines are used by the
paediatric community, they've confirmed that, and of
course, we've mobilised a group of clinical leads from
New South Wales to be part of the paediatric improvement
collaborative to make sure that the work was reflective
also of some of the needs that we had in terms of updates
of standards.

program, it's a program that is different in nature from
the paediatric improvement program, and that's why we've
put it in the statement. What we do with the NSQIP program

extract data from the electronic records, we ask patients

anaesthetists and other clinicians involved in surgery and

a benchmark compared to not just the participating sites in
New South Wales but also participating sites in the US and
in Canada, so that they can actually compare their practice
with an international benchmark and then identify where
they need to improve.

mobilise clinicians to look at data and self-identify
things that they can do locally to improve on some of those
outcomes.

collaborative.

what was initially planned and funded.

DR WATERHOUSE: Q. In those circumstances, are local

A. They can do that if they want and the tools - you

Q. Let's have a look now at paragraph 103. So this

What actions are taken if an evaluation is positive in the

for scale, we need to change some of, you know, its
characteristics, maybe we don't have the right technology
yet - you know, there's various reasons that would explain
why something that worked locally is not reproduced
somewhere else, but it could also be that the program needs
to be adapted to various contexts, because the spread test
is important because it tells us if something worked just
because, you know, you had a really dedicated group of
clinicians that somehow made it work, even though it was
a challenge to implement, or it informs us that there are

a rural versus a metropolitan setting, it could be the size

So when an evaluation of spread tells us that it's not

contexts, or is this truly a challenge in terms of
demonstrating the effectiveness of the program?
You know, things may not spread or scale not because

Q. Can there be cultural differences that influence

receptivity of different contexts to an innovation but also
the barriers that will come in the way and the things that
need to be worked out before we start to implement. So

Q. Would you have a look at paragraph 107 for me. I just

evaluation and the more dynamic situation modelling that
you're planning?
A. Yeah, so what we want to do is to really be able to
mobilise our evaluation teams to identify very early when
an implementation program is not going in the right
direction, when we need to make some adjustments to make
those programs a success.
It's really important because it's not true that you
always design things in a perfect way right from the start,
and that rapid evaluation enables us to tell local teams,
you know, "You may not be implementing the program the
right way", or, "Maybe we need to stop for a while, raise
the local capability, work on sponsorship or culture, and
then come back to make sure that we use the limited
resources we have for innovation in a way that really would
be effective."
When I say "agile", it's really about being able to
mobilise ourselves quickly. So if a district says, "We're
struggling", we should be able to mobilise resources
quickly, evaluate things, give them some feedback, move on.
In terms of the dynamic simulation modelling, that's
about predicting what's going to happen. We're lucky
because we live in a time where data computing capability
has really increased and we can increasingly do modelling
that is almost a replica of the healthcare system and the
way things move within the healthcare system. That can
better inform us in the future about the potential impact

of some of those new models and new technologies, but also
potential unintended consequences that we need to take care
of.
You know, if we implement something that has got an
impact on emergency department functioning, but ends up
putting more pressures on the beds on the wards, for the
entire system it may not be as positive as if we just look
at the emergency department's impacts.
So dynamic simulation modelling helps us to better
understand the interdependencies in the system and propose
to the system innovations that we know overall will have
a good impact in addition to the - you know, the already
trialled kind of processes within specific clinical units.
Q. How do you gather information for that modelling?
A. It's by linking different types of data. So we know
we've got intensive care data, emergency department
datasets, hospitalisation datasets. We've got workforce
data we can put in the mix, financial data. There's
increasingly capacity in the system to link different types
of information and then being able to provide that dynamic
simulation modelling.
But this being said, the clinical input is extremely
important because it's the clinicians that ultimately tell
us, you know, "If we do it this way, this task takes five
hours. If we do it that way, we can reduce it to one", you
know? And then we put the right parameters in the model to
have something that's not just based on historical data but
also based on what it could look like if the innovation is
successful. And that clinical input is absolutely
fundamental and that's why we feel that ACI is an
organisation that needs to use those tools because we've
got the clinical foundation to really get those kinds of
models right.

DR WATERHOUSE: Q. If we can go to paragraph 110,
please. Just roll down to subparagraph c. So you talk
there about prioritising innovations that are potential
game changers. Can you give us some examples of game
changers that have been identified to date?
A. There are obviously a few in virtual care, for
example, when studies demonstrated that some types of
remote monitoring would really help to reduce length of
stay in hospital, for example, or when remote monitoring or
virtual care would enable us to avoid hospitalising
patients by sending them back home instead, with the
appropriate technology that would enable us to track them.
But there also are the game changers in the advanced
therapeutics space where we can see that some new
treatments actually are at times costly, but can prevent
many episodes of illnesses and hospitalisation, and
therefore, they're game changers, because for some of them
it's a single treatment or a very short course of treatment
that can prevent a few years of the more traditional type
of treatments. That's really a game changer because it,
you know, completely changes the way we think about things.
I mean, the advances in cystic fibrosis are a good
example of that, where those treatments are really
positively impacting the health, the quality of life, you
know, of patients, of people with cystic fibrosis, and we
can see it is having an impact on the type of services we
need to provide for them as well. So they're truly
changing the game, you know, and that's something that we
need to increasingly be proactive about, provide the right
assessment and then design model that would support their
integration going forward.
Q. You mentioned there about requiring system changes,
and obviously ACI would not be responsible for all of
those, but what sorts of changes have had to be made to
accommodate new game changers like this?
A. Well, I think that maybe I will talk about CAR-T cells
again, you know, those cells attacking cancers. We knew
the technology was coming, but we also knew that to treat
patients with those technologies in the right way, we had
to somehow design things differently in terms of, you know,
what would be the referral patterns, when would we want to

provide them with those treatments, what kind of outpatient
follow-up would we have to do afterwards?
What we did is to work with relevant branches in the
ministry, with the local districts, and basically co-design
with them what would be the right processes to ensure good
access to those treatments.
It's going to be - well, it was the same with
Telestroke, you know, we really had to assess how it was
changing care, because obviously if you see a patient but
you can't access the actual technology that would enable
you to transmit the images to the hub, then you can't
provide Telestroke, and that, therefore, required at times
to even redesign the places where some instruments were
located within emergency departments in some of those
hospitals.
So those are the kinds of things that we increasingly
work with the system, giving them the support to provide
the redesign, but ultimately, of course, it's the local
districts and the local hospitals that, you know, do make
the change physically and from a process perspective, at
the local level.

challenges. I'm going to just highlight a few of these.

models of care, and b deals with local health districts
that are working in isolation and developing their own
models of care. Isn't there a place for local health
districts to develop their own models of care because they

we're talking about here is work that redesigned the entire
model of care that is produced at the state level. And in
some areas, you know, the evidence is quite clear, there
shouldn't be a big variation between local, you know,
processes and models of care, and we need to find a way,
then, to tell the local districts, you know, "This is
there, just adapt it to your local area, but we're very
confident this is the best model for your clinicians".
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Professor, would you mind - in

actual example of - in relation to subparagraph b, for

by LHDs that aren't brought to your attention and the

because I feel that it's happening in many different
clinical areas, but we're really talking about, you know,
models of care where clinicians would be mobilised for

starting to agree on what is the right way to deliver care,

a difficulty we face." It would really help me if there
was a more concrete example of what you're talking about
here rather than the general?
A. It's a difficulty because the amount of resources we
have to dedicate to mobilise clinicians, write up models of
care, is limited.
Q. Sure.

efforts in actually supporting adoption of those models of
care at the local level. And that's why, at the ACI, we're
working now with other states not to duplicate a model of
care if there's already a very good spinal cord injury or
maternity model of care developed in another state, and we
