locally adapted, but by avoiding redoing many of the steps
that they've taken to develop those models of care.
So we need to be more systematic at making sure that
we know what the districts are working on so that at times
we let them come up with the first, you know, draft and
design of specific clinical guidance, but also to make sure
that once they know we're working on a statewide model,
they don't invest all of the time required to mobilise
clinicians to produce one at the local level in addition to
that statewide one. Then we can mobilise resources to
support dissemination in the system, the appropriate

engagement with clinicians, and really the effort that's
required to support adoption locally. That's really our
goal.
Q. Okay. Well, this is your statement: "Models
developed by LHDs are not always brought to the attention
of the system" - what's an example of that?
A. It could be that a local district has developed their
own optimising surgical theatre guideline, when we already
have one that gives key elements that need to be considered
to make operating theatres more efficient.
Q. And this only comes to the attention of the system,
what, anecdotally or --
A. Either through the consolidation and then the work
that we do at the state level and then we realise that many
districts have developed in parallel similar kinds of
tools, or at times, it comes out if, you know, they tell us
that they already have a model of care following the
consultation.
Q. Well, just on that, wouldn't this be solved by
a monthly meeting where all new models of care that LHDs
are developing are discussed?
A. Well, it's - I think it's part of it, but it's also
about the commitment of the governance structures to
surface those and be transparent about it. It's not just
about collaborating. At times, it's about committing to
coordinate things. We certainly are committed to that
because the reality is that to run a healthcare system like
NSW Health, you need hundreds of clinical guidance
documents and models of care and they need to be up to
date.
Q. You don't need to go into specifics about this but
does that mean there are instances of some LHDs
deliberately not sharing models of care they're working on?
A. I think there's different drivers for that. Sometimes
it's just that clinicians may take the initiative to do it
and it doesn't quite surface up to the clinical governance
structures quickly, so that happens. Sometimes, to be
honest, it's universities that are reaching out to specific
clinical areas and starting to work on some of those models
of care. And at times, it's because they're required for
accreditation purposes or for other regulatory purposes,
and all of those things are things we can work on as
a system. The statement here is really a desire and

a commitment to reduce the burden that all of those models
of care impose on our system so that we can mobilise more
resourcing to actually implement them.
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. So the main concern, by the sound of
it, is duplication of resources or effort; is that correct?
A. Yes.
Q. But is it possible also that there may be more buy-in
from clinicians if they've personally been involved in
investigating and developing the model themselves?
A. Well, that's where championing and other things we
could do in collaboration can actually make a real
difference. If everybody agrees that we need one clinical
practice guide in a certain area and then local districts
work on translating it in terms of local processes, and
everybody agrees to that, I think we can achieve a more
coordinated approach, like in the English NHS, for example.
There's lots of examples where you can see that different
levels can actually contribute in a coordinated way with
other more locally driven levels, so that you avoid
duplication, and instead you increase tailorisation and
localisation of the guidelines.
Q. In paragraph c you refer to reluctance of local
communities and clinical groups to adopt or support
innovative models, and then further down, at f, it's
a similar issue of reluctance to incorporate successful
pilots into business as usual. What do you see as the
driver of this challenge or these challenges?
A. There's a lot of different drivers and, of course,
culture is one --
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, do you mean the drivers of the
reluctance or --
DR WATERHOUSE: Of the reluctance, yes.
THE WITNESS: So culture is one. Training of clinicians
and the way they're trained and the way they've practised
for a very long time is a driver of that. At times it's
also perception about, you know, what is the right care,
surgical versus non-surgical, home care versus
hospitalisation. Then, of course, there's the complexity
of the interaction between patients' expectations and what
clinicians feel they need to do for patients.

There's financial drivers to that, there's regulatory
drivers to that at times, and, of course, the paramount of
safety is really something that also at times is
a challenge for organisations like ours that have to
demonstrate that we can do things in a different way, in
more innovative ways, and it's still safe for patients, and
as the times, to be honest, even safer from the perspective
of preventing complications.
So it is complex to change clinical practice because
clinical practice is made of habit, it's made of - you
know, the word says it, "practice", you know, you get
better and better from a clinical perspective when you do
more surgeries of a certain way, and if the evidence
changes and suddenly you have to practise in a different
way, then it's challenging for those providers. So there's
a lot of different drivers but it's also part of the nature
of delivering health care.
Q. Let's move on to the opportunities in paragraph 113 --

assessment of potential innovations, et cetera, I think we

here, you've got data over there, you know, workforce data,
some other data, diagnostic data, whatever, but we don't
have a system that integrates that together; is that what
you mean by --

demonstrated that to manage personal protective equipment,
for example, we needed to link different types of
information to be able to predict the amount of masks that

something different, who knows --

Q. -- but anyway, I'll believe you.

A. My experience in other countries as well suggests that
we've got a strong foundation, but now it's the types of

relates to management of the system so that we're better
able to really provide advice about the right allocation of
resources to promote innovation and that's what that
statement is pushing for.
Q. We'll no doubt get into this in more detail later, but
to just get a few basic things in, and so we know what
we're talking about, when you use the term "artificial
intelligence", what do you mean?
A. It's a very good question, because it can mean many
different things, and in this case, it can mean - and I'm
talking about artificial intelligence techniques, so it can

but once they're derived, they're just automation of, you

times it could be that there's truly an artificial
intelligence software constantly learning about how to
better read wounds or x-rays or other imaging.
Q. That's sometimes called "machine learning", is it?
A. Yes.
Q. That's raw data in, the machine gets --
A. That's one --
Q. -- learns more?
A. That's one of the methods of artificial intelligence,

Q. And I think a subset of that is, like, neural
networks, where the more data you put in --
A. Yes.
Q. -- the machine actually ultimately gives you an answer

A. And refines the algorithm so - or other signal that

That's where some of those tools are learning whilst others
are based on artificial intelligence techniques but then
fixed in time. In health care, mostly it's fixed
algorithms developed through artificial intelligence that
we're seeing at the moment.

Q. And if I were to ask you, which I am, as to what are
the areas where artificial intelligence in the broad scope
we've just discussed might have an impact on the healthcare
system, can I ask you what they would be? One I've read
about obviously is opportunities for diagnostics, radiology
and pathology?
A. Yes.
Q. Can you explain a bit about that - looking at
pictures, et cetera. That's one area?
A. Yes. So one obvious area is diagnostics because, you
know, radiology, we're talking about scans and films that
have millions of pixels and therefore, analysing those
millions of pixels requires artificial intelligence to be
involved. It's the same with pathology where the movements
of, you know, different molecules in different tests can be
really, you know, enhanced by artificial intelligence
techniques.
But there are other areas where artificial
intelligence can really impact health care as well and --
Q. Predictions, you mentioned that before, predictive
technology?
A. Yes. Yes, predictions by looking at different
measures, you know, and multiple measures changing all at
the same time and capturing signals that maybe human beings
are not as quick to capture, but there's also --
Q. Like, for example, the patient's data going into the
machine and the machine --
A. Early signal of deterioration --
Q. -- sending a message to the doctor or clinicians and
the nurses, or whoever, saying "This person might be about
to go into kidney failure or sepsis", or something like
that?
A. Yes. There are tools that have been developed through
artificial intelligence that do exactly that. They're
currently being refined and evaluated and tested, but yes,
it can be an adjuvant to clinical decision, because it
captures early changes that again wouldn't be evident if
you just looked at the patient without mixing together
a lot of different pieces of information.
Another area is drug discoveries, research.

Increasingly artificial intelligence can help to reduce the
time that it takes to identify which molecules would be
a good candidate for treating that specific condition and
guide the repurposing of drugs so that we, you know,
respond to some illnesses where the current therapies
available are not quite responding to the needs.
In the past, we would have to do that manually. You
know, drug per drug, testing with new indications.
Artificial intelligence really helps to speed that process
and identify the most likely candidates to work in the
repurposing, and it's going to be the same in many
different areas of proteomics, metabolomics where there's
a lot of proteins in the body and artificial intelligence
is increasingly helping us to understand what are the
configurations that are a marker of a certain condition or
the evolution of disease, and therefore we need to get
ready to better assess those technologies using artificial
intelligence and wrap them around the right governance
framework so that it reaps the benefits, whilst we also
manage the risks associated with those going forward, and
that's why the artificial intelligence task force was
established.
Q. Right. So diagnostics, predictions like early warning
systems?
A. Research and discovery.
Q. Drug development?
A. Yes.
Q. What else could there be?
A. Back of office management of some tasks. There's
literature --
Q. Funding models?
A. There's literature emerging in many different areas
and that includes --
Q. There could be an algorithm that solves this entire
Inquiry.
A. This is outside of my specific area of expertise --
Q. Yes, it's outside of mine too.
A. -- but I know that there's a lot of trials in many
areas that relate to managing the healthcare system as
well.

Q. And there are more basic uses of artificial
intelligence like chatbots that remind people, "Don't
forget to take the drugs that you've been prescribed", that
sort of thing?
A. Some of them are indeed integrated into medical
devices at times to support, you know, patient behaviours
and adherence to some treatments as well.
Q. And in your role as head of the task force, artificial
intelligence task force that has just been set up, I know
you haven't finalised your terms of reference yet, but --
A. They are.
Q. -- what are the key risks that you see to health from
artificial intelligence?
A. So from what we know in the literature and various
frameworks adopted internationally, obviously, you know,
privacy is extremely important, you know, management of
information is really one of those. But also regulatory
frameworks, we need to better understand for some of those
tools what would be the implications from a medicolegal
perspective. We need to ensure really that when we assess
those technologies we consider all of those risks before we
start to integrate them into mainstream clinical settings.
Q. There's still a risk of machine error like there's
a risk of human error at the moment?
A. Yes. And one of our roles is to survey the literature
and compare when algorithms have been compared to clinical
decisions, and then reflect on how do we need to use our
clinicians and the expertise that they have to be enhanced
by those technologies when we find that there are some
tasks that those technologies can do in a more consistent
way. And that's the kind of translation that we will have
to do, but again within our safety frameworks, which are
extremely important from a health perspective.
Q. Your task force, I think I read, is time limited at
the moment. What does that mean?
A. Oh --
Q. I know what it means --
A. -- we don't know --
Q. -- but what does it mean specifically?
A. We don't know how long it's going to be there for.

The goal is to accelerate a lot of the changes within the
system across different organisations because artificial
intelligence, just like data and information, is not going
to be something managed only by one team within a complex
system like NSW Health, you know, there's going to be
implications for workforce, finances, clinical settings,
et cetera. And for the task force --
Q. You wouldn't have set the task force up for fun --
A. No.
Q. -- given the number of meetings you have to go to?
A. Yes.
Q. Is AI amongst the biggest challenges/opportunities
coming to the health system generally?
A. It is top priority for us, so that we get ready for
a lot of the developments that will appear in the coming
years. And the task force is there so that every component
of the New South Wales health system now starts to think
about what is it that we need to do now to manage the
current challenges related to AI, and how do we get ready
for the next few years? And that can be in terms of,
again, regulation-specific policies, clinical information
systems, you know, there's a lot of different aspects that
need to be progressed and we're just bringing all of the
leaders from the system to co-design it together.
Q. So one of the research institutes described to us in a
meeting that the number of gene therapies, cancer
therapies, precision medicine therapies that are coming,
literally within the next 12 months to five years, is like
a tsunami hitting the system - AI is like a second tsunami
or building on that tsunami in terms of its potential
impacts on the system?
A. Yeah, so, as I was saying, in terms of research, AI is
going to increasingly - you know, it's going to increase
the speed of change. So for gene therapies, for example,
AI is really enabling us now to analyse millions of gene
mutations and better understand the potential of some of
the therapies. So that means that the pipeline of
innovation is going to rapidly increase and we need to be
ready to harness that. And that's the goal of the task
force, to put in place the right, you know, administrative,
clinical engagement, data infrastructure, et cetera,
processes so that we take that wave for the benefit of the
system and the population of New South Wales.

Q. Do you want to be cheeky and tell me how much money
you need to be right on top of all of this?
A. I wouldn't be able to say that.
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. I had a few questions myself about AI
so I might just cover off on those now. How was the AI
task force that you're co-chairing selected?
A. So we did an expression of interest across the system,
asking chief executives of organisations of local
districts, of various stakeholders across the system, to
identify their key people that would be able to come to the
task force and share their expertise but also come back to
those organisations and be the leaders of change. Because
we're really talking about a task force that will not be
able to do all of the work on its own. It's really about
leveraging the work of pathology, eHealth, ACI, the local
districts and we've got a really good representation of all
of those organisations.
Q. Does it include external experts who actually develop
AI programs?
A. There are some, and we also have other mechanisms for
us to be connected with that, so we've got a living
evidence table on AI that's available on our website and
constantly updated, but we're also part of the artificial
intelligence, you know, national network, where we receive
information about the key developments, and we've been
a member of that national group for four years.
Q. And one of the roles of the task force, will that be
to look at the lack of integrated data for modelling,
et cetera?
A. I think the task force will look at what is the
potential that AI would give us to have a more streamlined
integration but also potentially how can we use new methods
that would protect privacy, reduce some of the risks
related with linkage through designing synthetic datasets,
for example. And by synthetic datasets, I really mean
datasets where we could still analyse data and find
relationships, but nobody in that dataset is an actual real
person, if you see what I mean. It's almost like you tweak
the data so that it preserves the association so that you
can do the studies, but nobody's information is
identifiable anymore, and, of course, AI can help us to
develop new ways to analyse data like this.

Q. The task force is charged with developing a framework.
What will that framework cover?
A. That framework we intend would cover what is the
regulatory approaches; what are the key priority areas we
need to explore; what are some of the risks and issues;
what are the clinical applications that we want also to
prioritise and explore; what are the applications that may
actually help the system to run efficiently as well? The
framework should help us to give guidance to the system for
the next few years about, you know, accompanying that
introduction of those technologies in different parts of
the system, or through different devices and technologies
that we use otherwise.
Q. We've talked a bit about resistance to change, and you
identified this as being an area of profound change. What
is ACI or the task force doing to manage this anticipated
change and what you can expect to be the resistance to it?
A. So, I mean, establishing the task force and building
the framework is, of course, the first step. We are --
Q. I'm talking specifically about how are you going to
manage the resistance to this profound change?
A. I think it's about being transparent about truly
what's being demonstrated there. So what is the evidence;
what is the comparative effectiveness of a medical device
that uses or not; what is the comparative effectiveness
between human based processes versus processes that are
enhanced by AI?
But it's also about - going to be about working with
the developers of AI so that there's more transparency
about the AI tools, because clinicians will want to know
how is this working, and we cannot propose to them a black
box where they can't see how is this algorithm arriving at
a certain result.
The challenge, of course, is that for some of those AI
tools, it's very difficult to explain how it works, because
it is, you know, a neuro system or a deep learning system,
and therefore, it's going to be a challenge for some of
those applications. It will have to be through research
and trials so that we will demonstrate that those things
work, just like we do for pharmaceuticals, and I think that
then clinicians would be willing to explore using some of
those tools.

Q. If we could just go to paragraph 113, you say at the
beginning there, in the second sentence:
There are opportunities for greater
linkages between the delivery arm of NSW
Health and the innovation arm ...
Can you clarify what you mean by those two arms?
A. I really mean between ACI and local health districts
and local hospitals. We need to continue to strengthen
that relationship and that collaboration. You know,
there's no point in having a central agency doing all of
that work, assessing what's emerging in the literature,
what's emerging in different clinical settings, and then
not have a system based approach to ensure that it
translates into clinical practice, you know, and therefore,
I think we need to further that linkage through different
ways, and that's really a commitment that we have.
Q. But there is already a lot of innovation happening at
a district level. It's not all coming from ACI, is it?
A. Absolutely, absolutely.
Q. You talk also about no jurisdiction having fully
achieved this. Are there other jurisdictions you're aware
of that are doing it better that we can learn from?
A. There are some that I would consider gold standard,
some American HMOs, for example, that really have been able
to fully integrate a lot of their innovation ecosystem with
their delivery arms. I think that we sit in a good place
at the moment in New South Wales and we can build on that
platform, but we're not achieving the level that some of
those systems are achieving at the moment.
Q. Did I hear you say HMOs?
A. HMOs, or other types of organisations in the US, some
systems in Canada as well. There are European systems
where they've established quite embedded innovation
processes. We're scanning those to be informed by them and
learn from them, either through our international expert
advisory group or through the international scanning that
we do otherwise.
Q. And by "HMO" do you mean health maintenance
organisation?
A. Yes.

Q. In 113a, in subparagraph a there, you refer to ABF as
being a barrier. But ABF is not actually an impediment to
change, is it? Would it be fair to say there's nothing to
stop a district adopting a model of care that's more
efficient, even if it doesn't translate to counting towards
hospital based activity?
A. That's correct. There's nothing that stops districts
from doing this, and there's even ways within the National
Health Reform Agreement that would allow for some of those
innovative models to be delivered, explored and funded.
I think that a lot of it is because of culture and habit
and at times people take for granted that the new model
will disrupt things and therefore it's perceived as not
being supported by the current funding model.
Q. So it's a perception that's out in the system --
A. At times.
Q. -- is that correct?
A. At times it is.
Q. You talk about blended reimbursement approaches. Can
you explain what you mean by that?
A. Yeah. So blended reimbursement approaches are when
you start to combine funding that comes per capita, for
example - you know, number of patients within a certain
roster. A certain amount would come from activity, where
if you give more vaccines, you get paid for those vaccines.
Some of it is block funding and, of course, block funding
is already present in NSW Health, but we need to find a way
to use it strategically for the purpose of innovation. And
at times also there could be other funding models or
reimbursement models that are based on outcomes, for
example.
So blended models are really models where you use
outcome based, activity based, capitation models as well as
block funding to provide a flexible approach to clinical
settings so that they make the decision based on the
patient's needs, not so much, you know, just to produce
more services.
Q. Let's scroll down to subparagraph e.
A. Did you say e, sorry?
Q. Yes, e for "echo"?
A. Thanks.

Q. You talk there about greater rationalisation of the
vast numbers of local models in the second-last line there.
How does ACI plan to achieve that given the extent that
you've highlighted of the variation in uptake and districts
doing their own thing?
A. So the first thing is that we've started to revise our
own internal processes to develop those models of care and
those clinical practice guides. We're talking about
hundreds of models that we need to keep current, keep up to
date, and therefore, we needed to ensure that we had
a systematic approach internally first, to make sure that
people would believe that our models are always, you know,
current, valid and should be used, and we're implementing
at the moment those approaches.
We're also reducing our own burden by collaborating
with other states and we've established collaborative
platforms that enable us to do that. We actually led the
establishment of those platforms and I've been the chair of
some of those committees for a while.
And then we need to discuss and engage in a
conversation with local districts about the reasons why
sometimes they develop their own models or want to
replicate some of the work that we've done so that we
better understand the drivers and then we can collectively
find solutions.
I think the reality around the world is that many
organisations are now struggling to maintain those
guidelines, because we've covered the various clinical
areas and now it's coming back at us because, you know,
some of them are five years old, we need to update them.
This is putting a pressure on organisations that in reality
should be looking at the future, innovation, and now we're
caught at revising what in reality is standardising care,
and for us that's not the right balance. We need more time
for innovation and to reduce the impost of maintaining -
the maintenance of those standards, and to be informed by
that, we've also been active participants in some
international groups that are looking at different ways to
generate evidence and generate guidelines, as well as
national groups that do so, such as the evidence task force
that is led at a national level.
Those are the different ways we've put together to

make sure that we've got best practice in that space and
can, you know, rebalance our efforts towards innovation and
a bit less towards standardisation.
Q. If we scroll down, please, to subparagraph h, this
refers to streamlining decision-making in government and
improving links with other government bodies. I want to
ask you about a scenario that's a bit closer to home than
the big sort of enterprise investment and trade, et cetera.
We heard evidence last week from the chief executive
of a local health district that suggested that the ACI
clinical networks should be more involved in providing
advice before state contracts are negotiated for clinical
products.
We then heard from the chief executive of HealthShare
NSW, who said that technical evaluation committees will
decide if advice is needed from ACI when they're
considering entering into a state contract for a clinical
product, so that the ACI may or may not be involved
depending on what the product is.
Then subsequently we heard from the chief procurement
officer who said that the ACI has a role in monitoring the
patient outcomes that are related to clinical products that
have been procured under state contract. So those are, if
you like, three slightly contrasting views in terms of
ACI's role, but all highlighting where they see ACI either
should or does play a role.
So how would you describe the ACI's role in
procurement of clinical products on statewide contracts
that are negotiated by HealthShare?
A. By HealthShare?
Q. Yes.
A. So currently, our involvement is through providing
clinical advice in specific areas when, you know, we have
to, for example, provide contracts that would impact on our
surgeons in the state or when they're contracting devices
or instruments that, you know, would have an impact on
clinical care. What we do is that we either mobilise
a network or we identify clinicians, you know, to be part
of those assessment committees, and inform their processes
from the clinical perspective, okay?

So far, every time we were asked, we provided that
support. We've had significant work with HealthShare in
the surgical space. We have significant involvement with
HealthShare in other areas that relate to disability and
the types of procurement that need to be done for people
living with disability that may need support - nutrition,
you know, many areas where there are interventions that
really would relate to what is being procured.
We're not involved in pharmaceutical, which is really
under the remit of the Clinical Excellence Commission. And
at times what we've done also is to do evidence reviews to
really understand also what are the current practices
internationally with regards to procurement for some of
those and what is the level of evidence about the risks or
benefits of changing some of those procurement approaches.
You know, you may want to go to more or less options
for certain types of clinicians as part of, you know, the
list of products available in the system, and it needs to
be based on evidence.
So, so far, this is really the way we have supported
HealthShare in its work.
Q. So, to be clear, that's on an as-needs basis when you
are asked for advice. Do you ever offer up advice on some
sort of clinical area that you're working on to make
HealthShare aware of something so that if they're looking
at state contracts, they can take that advice into account?
A. I would say this is not an area where we have had
proactive work ongoing to be able to, you know, proactively
alert them of this, apart from if there's clearly the
emergence of a new technology, a new prosthesis, et cetera,
then our clinicians are alerting us that, you know, "This
is coming", and then we inform HealthShare about that,
providing the advice ahead of time. But it remains an
ad hoc perspective because it really depends on our
clinicians identifying those emerging innovations as having
an impact on potential procurement activities.
Q. Do you think that ACI should take a more consistent
role in terms of being involved routinely rather than
ad hoc?
A. I think that that's something we could explore.
There's obviously work implications and potential
reorientation or reprioritisation of some of the work, if

we were to do this on a more systematic basis, but that's
something that we could explore in discussions with
HealthShare and other partners.
Q. In terms of the monitoring function, once a statewide
contract is in place, how does ACI monitor the effects of
the clinical products that are being procured this way?
A. So I would say that it does that in an indirect way.
We're not the organisation in charge of, you know, post
marketing or post commercialisation monitoring. But we do
have clinical variation work where - and contribution to
clinical registries, for example, where the data that we
collect would reflect on changes in outcomes and sometimes
it can actually be related to a specific procedure or
a specific device that is used in certain clinical areas.
It is limited. It is not systematic, and it really
depends on the current measures that are measured as part
of those registries or as part of our clinical variation
work. But certainly, it's not systematic and it's not for
the purpose of alerting the system that, you know, there
would be anything wrong with those medical devices. We
track outcomes overall to identify needs for innovation.
At times, it can be related to specific devices or
prostheses, but the purpose is not to monitor, you know,
the outcomes of those procurement processes.
Q. And finally, in paragraph 114, your statement ends
with the description of the clinical innovation and
research division having strong foundation but identifying
that there's always room for improvement. Going forward,
what are you most optimistic about in terms of innovation
for the New South Wales health system?
A. I've written that statement because I'm extremely
proud of the work that the teams have done over the last
few years through the pandemic, really keeping focus on
innovation, keeping focus on identifying new ways to work,
engaging with very broad and big clinical groups, you know,
to ensure that we design things that will harness
innovation but in a way that fits with clinical practice
and clinical expectations.
I believe that there's going to be ongoing
improvements in surgery and value based surgery, and that's
really a key priority program for us and we continue to
push.

I believe that there's going to be massive disruptions
coming out of personalised medicine and we're currently
working with our clinical networks so that it's not just
a responsibility of the genetic, you know, clinical group,
it's really something that will impact other clinical areas
as well and they need to pay attention to that.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. What do you mean by "disruptions"?
A. I mean technologies that will suddenly force people to
think differently and will challenge the way we provide
care at the moment. You know, how do you link a patient
with a specific clinical condition - and they may be the
only one in a hospital that year - to connect them with the
right treatment that, you know, may be available somewhere
else in the system? That's not the way we work at the
moment, just to give an example. So personalisation of
medicine will have its challenges and we need to work
across the different clinical areas and networks to get
ready for that.
Q. Is one of those challenges cost?
A. Cost can be a challenge, of course, because some of
those technologies are expensive. Sometimes, they are
expensive but we need to compare them with the current
investments and sometimes lifelong investments, but those
lifelong investments, you understand, will be in many
different places, many different cost centres, whilst, as
a single technology, there may be a single one, and that's
a disruption on its own and we need to support the system
to make the right arbitration, but also reorganise the way
care is planned and delivered so that sometimes we can make
those decisions to allocate towards those expensive
therapies as well.
